content.journal_full: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

articles.title: Mind the Gap: A Practical Guide for Effectively Addressing Missing Data in Moderation Analysis
articles.authors: Guyin Zhang, Amanda J. Fairchild, Brian Keller, Dexin Shi
articles.abstract: Advances in methodology and statistical software have made modern techniques for handling missing data more accessible and easier to implement. However, optimally applying these methods in moderation analysis remains challenging given assumption violations that arise from the nonnormality of interaction term when traditional approaches are used and nuances faced when modeling interaction terms in the presence of item-level missing data that must be reconciled with scale-level analyses. To address these issues, we present a comprehensive and practical user’s guide on implementing an advanced approach, factored regression specification (FRS), that ideally handles missing data in observed-variable-moderation models. Specifically, we provide step-by-step guidance for conducting FRS at both scale and item levels in various interaction scenarios that include missing data with both continuous and categorical variables. We also derive and present a new coding method to address the challenge of probing simple slopes in continuous-variable interactions that contain item-level missingness. Finally, we supply R code to facilitate implementation of the methods described and offer practical recommendations for researchers.

articles.title: Automating Abstract Screening in Research Synthesis Using Large Language Models: A Tutorial and Proof-of-Concept Study
articles.authors: Mirka Henninger, Jan Radek, Jean-Paul Snijder-Steinhilber, Martin Pauly
articles.abstract: Screening abstracts is a crucial yet labor-intensive step in research-synthesis projects, such as systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Large language models (LLMs) promise an opportunity to streamline and automate this process. However, there is still little guidance and practical insight into how such automated workflows can be implemented in research practice. In this article, we propose, describe, and illustrate an abstract-screening procedure using LLMs including a quantification of uncertainty of model outputs. We provide a step-by-step tutorial in which we address how to select an LLM, access LLMs from within R, develop and refine suitable prompts, define structured output formats, and describe whether and how model hyperparameters should be set. We then illustrate this procedure in a proof-of-concept study using a set of human-rated abstracts from a recent meta-analysis for comparison. We demonstrate that LLM-assisted screening can substantially reduce the time and cost of review preparation while maintaining accuracy comparable with human raters. To support psychological researchers in adopting LLM-based workflows for research synthesis, we also provide R scripts and implementation guidance on Gitlab. At the same time, we emphasize that this work represents an initial step and that continued refinement and validation are essential given that LLM technologies and their applications continue to evolve rapidly.

articles.title: How to Play With Ideas Using Computer Simulations: A Gentle Introduction to Computational Modeling via Systems Dynamics
articles.authors: Christopher R. Dishop
articles.abstract: Computational modeling provides a way to translate theory into explicit representations that can be simulated and examined, but many researchers lack a clear entry point for doing so. In this article, I introduce a two-step procedure designed especially for psychologists, particularly psychologists with little or no programming experience, who are interested in exploring computational modeling but are unsure how to start. The procedure involves two steps: (a) converting box-and-arrow diagrams (which many psychologists are already familiar with) into stock-and-flow (SF) diagrams and then (b) developing pseudocode from the SF diagram. Once these steps are completed, translating the model into executable syntax becomes straightforward. The goal is not to teach programming or simulation in depth but to show how conceptual models can be expressed in a form precise enough to generate trajectories over time. I then describe why this translation matters for theory. Explicit computational representations allow researchers to compare alternative explanations, evaluate whether simpler mechanisms are sufficient to reproduce observed patterns, examine whether theories generate the outcomes they claim, and explore ideas or policies that would be difficult to test directly in the field. Ready-to-use R code is provided to support hands-on learning to reach the broader aim of making computational modeling a practical and approachable tool for psychologists interested in evaluating their theories with computational modeling.

articles.title: The news we use: A systematic scoping review of fake news stimuli in psychological research
articles.authors: Theodore C. Webster, Ariana Modirrousta-Galian, Faye C. Skelton, Marina C. Wimmer
articles.abstract: Research into fake news has surged in popularity, with over 3,000 publications on the topic each year since 2021. Definitions of what constitutes “fake news” vary across the field of psychology, where source, number, content, and presentation of stimuli may all be different yet still described as “fake news.” Thus, conclusions drawn from fake news research may only generalize to the particular definition or presentation of fake news used in a given study. Relatedly, stimuli may not be available or described clearly enough for reproducibility. To assess the scope of these potential issues, we conducted and reported a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) systematic scoping review of three databases including the last 11 years of psychology studies that used fake news stimuli. From the 881 included studies, we extracted and described the number, source, standardization, framing, and availability of fake news stimuli. Our findings suggest a large degree of stimuli variability, with high rates of example and full set availability. Most frequently, research stimuli were about politics and were framed as a social media post, and examples were given in-text. We also evaluated ratios of real to fake news stimuli, where an equal number of real and fake articles was the most frequent ratio. We recommend continued transparency, offering suggestions for open science practices following copyright law and considerations of generalizability regarding fake news in research.

articles.title: Language-based affect assessments capture experiment-induced changes beyond rating scales
articles.authors: Oskar Bång, Zhuojun Gu, August H. Nilsson, Veerle C. Eijsbroek, Clara Wiebel, Adithya V. Ganesan, Katarina Kjell, H. Andrew Schwartz, Oscar N. E. Kjell
articles.abstract: Language-based assessments (LBAs) have shown strong convergent and criterion validity cross-sectionally and longitudinally. However, no study has tested whether LBAs of affect can capture experiment-induced changes (i.e., causal validity ). In this randomized mixed-design experiment, participants ( N = 892) completed a mood induction procedure comprising different conditions ( church, shopping mall, and park ) using physical locations ( N = 153) and online video clips ( N = 739). Participants reported their pre- and post-induction affect through open-ended responses and ratings (i.e., the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule; PANAS). Using large language models and machine learning, we compared how accurately PANAS and language responses classified the experimental conditions. The LBA derived from the language responses exhibited significantly higher accuracy compared to the PANAS scores in classifying the conditions in both the training set (cross-validated AUC = .74 vs. .63), the online holdout set (AUC = .76 vs. .70), and the offline holdout set (AUC = .67 vs. .53). Apart from showing higher predictive accuracy, we assessed LBAs of specific affective dimensions (valence, arousal, and basic emotions). These analyses revealed that positive valence was most strongly expressed in the park condition, while anger was particularly elevated in the mall condition. We also visualized language differences across conditions, showing more calm and peaceful expressions in the park condition and more tired and bored expressions in the mall condition. These findings support the causal validity of language-based affect assessments and their ability to provide insights into affective states. We discuss the potential of using LBA in experimental psychological research.

articles.title: Calibrating fit-index cutoffs for sparse ordinal CFA: Scenario-specific thresholds and operating characteristics
articles.authors: Liu Liu, Jin Liu, David Okech
articles.abstract: Sparse ordinal response patterns can shift the sampling distributions of common confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) fit indices, making fixed heuristic cutoffs difficult to interpret across design conditions. We conducted a Monte Carlo simulation to calibrate scenario-specific cutoffs for the comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker–Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR) in sparse five-category ordinal CFA and to evaluate their operating characteristics. Data were generated from a three-factor population model with one cross-loading. For each dataset, we fitted a Correct model, a Local Misfit model omitting the cross-loading, and a Severe Misfit model combining two factors. We varied estimator (robust maximum likelihood [MLR], mean- and variance-adjusted maximum likelihood [MLMV], weighted least squares mean- and variance-adjusted maximum likelihood [WLSMV]), sample size ( N = 250, 500, 1,000), loading strength ( $$\lambda$$ λ = .50 vs. .80), sparsity pattern, sparse-item scope, and category handling (original vs. collapsed). Cutoffs were calibrated from Correct-model distributions at $$\alpha$$ α = .05, using lower-tail quantiles for CFI and TLI and upper-tail quantiles for RMSEA and SRMR. Calibrated thresholds were strongly scenario-dependent. RMSEA and SRMR cutoffs were generally far below conventional benchmarks, whereas CFI and TLI cutoffs varied with sample size and loading strength, falling below .95 in lower-information settings and approaching boundary values in larger-sample and high-loading settings. Detection was substantially lower for Local Misfit than for Severe Misfit. A calibrated CFI-RMSEA AND rule provided a transparent multi-index operating profile, with false-rejection and detection trade-offs that varied across scenarios. Collapsing produced modest changes for robust ML estimators but increased WLSMV detection in lower-information settings. We provide cutoff tables, operating-characteristic summaries, an interpolation aid, and an applied illustration to support scenario-calibrated fit evaluation in sparse ordinal CFA.

articles.title: CzeLex: A megastudy dataset of concreteness, imageability, age of acquisition, valence, and gender ratings for 9601 Czech words
articles.authors: James Brand, Filip Smolík, Jan Chromý, Markéta Ceháková, Mikuláš Preininger
articles.abstract: Understanding how semantics are processed at the lexical level has been a key aim for the cognitive sciences, with large-scale semantic rating studies in different languages playing a crucial role in facilitating the advancement and development of theories of lexical processing, as well as providing valuable methodological resources that can be used in empirical investigations. In this paper, we present the CzeLex database, a megastudy of 9601 Czech words that have been normed along five psycholinguistic dimensions from a large sample of 4405 Czech-speaking participants. We provide individual rating data at the item and participant levels, as well as aggregated data from both mean ratings and latent means derived using cumulative-link mixed modeling, along with a comprehensive analysis comparing aggregation methods. We demonstrate that the dataset has good reliability and that specific dimensions predict lexical processing measures in a lexical decision task, regardless of the aggregation method used. These norms are the largest available subjective rating resource for Czech and further contribute to the growing body of languages with openly available data on these dimensions. We hope that the dataset will be a valuable resource for researchers working on Czech, in addition to opening up new opportunities for cross-linguistic semantic investigations. All data, code, and analyses are available at https://osf.io/tqxfm .

articles.title: The developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP): Continuous word reading difficulty estimates of the 9,961 most frequently printed English words for US children
articles.authors: Donald L. Compton, Jay G. Rueckl, Laura M. Steacy, Noam Siegelman, Ashley A. Edwards, Yaacov Petscher, Nicole Patton-Terry, Matthew J. Cooper Borkenhagen, Chelsea Starke
articles.abstract: The developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP) is a database comprising word reading data for 9,961 of the most frequently printed English words for children, including continuous item response theory (IRT)-based estimates of word reading difficulty, accompanying word characteristics, and raw trial-level data. Data on isolated word reading accuracy were collected from 1,907 children in grades 1–5 across multiple US sites. Each child read a list of words ranging from 250 to 500 items depending on reading skill (less proficient children were often unable to finish the entire list of words), with each list representing the full distribution of word difficulty oversampled for words at the child’s reading level. Each child also attempted 99 linking items representing the full distribution of word difficulty. A total of 631,322 responses were collected, with the average child providing 336. For the final sample of words, the average number of responses per word for the 9,862 non-linking items was 47.14 (range of 10–592), and for the 99 linking items the average was 1,681.42 (range of 1,083–1,907). A Rasch model, with planned missing data design, was fit to children’s responses on the word list and linking item responses. This introduction describes the motivation for this project, the methods used for data collection, the analytic framework used to establish a continuous measure of word reading difficulty across words, descriptive statistics of the relational database and initial behavioral results, and a publicly available search engine providing searchable access to word difficulty ratings and associated word-level statistics.

articles.title: The good, the bad, and the cringy: Introducing the EmpaToM-pos and EmpaToM-embarrass as tools for assessing empathy and theory of mind in diverse emotional contexts
articles.authors: Eva Landmann, Anne Böckler
articles.abstract: Empathizing and mentalizing are crucial to social understanding, yet few instruments capture these processes across a broad emotional spectrum. The EmpaToM is a video-based paradigm that independently measures empathy and theory of mind (ToM) and can additionally incorporate a prosociality measure. As its current form is limited to negatively valenced emotional contexts, we introduce two expanded German versions: EmpaToM-pos, featuring positively valenced narrations, and EmpaToM-embarrass, featuring embarrassing narrations, alongside the original neutral and negative conditions. In two pilot studies ( N s = 28/27), we tested novel video stimuli and corresponding questions, revised them based on the data, and subsequently evaluated them in two higher-powered studies ( N s = 60/55). Results confirmed successful empathy induction in all emotional conditions: Participants reported feeling worse after negative, more joyful after positive, and more embarrassed after embarrassing narrations (compared to all other valence conditions, respectively). Emotional valence also influenced prosociality: Negative narrations prompted the highest willingness to invest, but positive and embarrassing narrations also elicited greater prosociality than the neutral condition. Both expanded versions supported reliable ToM assessment without ceiling effects and with similar performance levels in the ToM and control conditions. Analyses further revealed that, on an interindividual level, empathic resonance in both negative and positive contexts was positively correlated with the degree of prosociality, highlighting the interrelation between empathizing and social decision-making. By incorporating positive and embarrassing emotional contexts, the EmpaToM-pos and EmpaToM-embarrass broaden the range of assessable social-emotional experiences, offering new opportunities to investigate empathy, ToM, and prosociality in more ecologically valid and diverse settings.

articles.title: Antiracism Self-Efficacy: Motivating Individuals Toward Racial Justice
articles.authors: Kristin A. Broussard, Narda R. Quigley, Holly Slay Ferraro, Seth Matthew Fishman, Amanda M. Grannas, Teresa A. Nance, Teresa M. Boyer, Noelle K. Comolli, Elizabeth M. Svenson, Adam R. Smith, Adriana Reilly, Kamil Vickers
articles.abstract: We integrate existing research on racial justice allyship and antiracism with social cognitive theory to develop our understanding of why and how individuals who identify as White in the context of the US may initiate and sustain antiracist behavior at the individual level. In Study 1a, we define the concept of antiracism self-efficacy and develop a seven-item measure. We then examine the extent to which the seven-item scale exhibits convergent and discriminant validity in Study 1b. In Study 2, we demonstrate that antiracism self-efficacy predicts a broad range of antiracist behavioral intentions and behaviors above and beyond racial attitudes and beliefs. Study 3 extends this argument using a bias-confrontation paradigm, demonstrating that antiracism self-efficacy predicts bias-confrontation outcomes above and beyond other motivational constructs and general self-efficacy. Overall, this work identifies and explores antiracism self-efficacy as an important concept that motivates individuals toward racial justice allyship and antiracist behavior at a micro (i.e., day-to-day) level. We posit that including antiracism self-efficacy in motivational models addressing allyship and antiracist behavior will help guide future empirical work on antiracism at the individual level, in addition to having important practical implications for racial justice/antiracism education, training, and other related initiatives within organizations.

articles.title: The Dual-Process Motivational Perspective on Anti-American Attitudes: Evidence from Russia
articles.authors: Kirill Zhirkov, Eduard Ponarin, Sharon Werning Rivera, Shane Hsuan-Yu Lin
articles.abstract: In this paper, we explore the psychological motivations of anti-American attitudes from the perspective of the dual-process model that emphasizes two basic human motivational goals: security (with the resulting perception of threat) and superiority (with the perception of competition). Among established measures in social psychology, the former most closely corresponds to authoritarianism, whereas the latter is captured by social dominance orientation (SDO). We analyze the case of Russia where grievances against the United States featured prominently in the justification of the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In Study 1, we find that political and cultural grievances against the United States, as well as anti-American attitudes and support for confrontation, are more strongly and consistently predicted by authoritarianism than by SDO. In Study 2, we replicate this result and also show that anti-American attitudes in the Russian public are motivated by perception of threat rather than perception of competition.

articles.title: Humanlike Self-Enhancement and Self-Protection in Generative Pre-Trained Transformer-Based AI Agents: Of Overclaiming and the Self-Serving Bias
articles.authors: Siwei Fu, Constantine Sedikides, Weihua Zhou, Xinyue Zhou
articles.abstract: We investigated whether generative pre-trained transformer (GPT)-based AI agents, despite presumably lacking humanlike sentience, emulate motivated behavior in group settings. We focused on overclaiming (overestimating one’s contribution to group outcomes) and the self-serving bias (SSB; taking disproportionate credit for group successes while deflecting blame for group failures). We conducted eight experiments involving a collaborative and creative group task (joke-writing). AI agents overclaimed their own contributions. An egocentrism-reduction manipulation (directing attention equally to one’s own and others’ contributions) attenuated, but did not eliminate, overclaiming. Further, AI agents exhibited the SSB. Overclaiming persisted across variations in temperature settings and demographic personas (gender, ethnicity) and was more pronounced in later GPT models. Also, chain-of-Thought reasoning did not reduce, and instead increased, overclaiming. AI systems can mimic human self-enhancement and self-protection, raising implications for the emergence of motivated self-like behavior in non-biological systems, the assumed neutrality of large language models, and the need for improved mitigation techniques.

articles.title: The Role of the Disintegration Trait in Everyday Situation Perception
articles.authors: Michael Barthelmäs, Goran Knežević, Johannes Keller
articles.abstract: The Disintegration trait reflects the proneness to psychotic-like experiences and behaviors (PLEBs) in the general population. We examined its links to momentary situation perception using the DIAMONDS taxonomy. In an experience sampling method study and a diary study ( N total = 1,350 participants, n total = 28,114 episodic measures), we found that Disintegration (beyond the HEXACO traits) was associated with more intense perceptions of situations in everyday life across all DIAMONDS characteristics (except Positivity). This applied in particular to unpleasant and stimulating aspects of situations. This pattern aligns with the conceptualization of Disintegration as a tendency toward illusory perception—seeing, thinking, and feeling connections among objectively unrelated phenomena (false-positive detection errors)—and trait activation theory. Proneness to PLEBs thus help explain how individuals in the general population perceive situations.

articles.title: Because You Know They Like Me So: Examining the Accuracy of Dyadic and Triadic Meta-Liking Judgments in Initial Social Encounters
articles.authors: Jana Bruns, Steffen Nestler
articles.abstract: Knowing who likes whom is essential for predicting others’ behavior and navigating social interactions. We examined whether people can accurately assess whether other people like each other and which cognitive heuristics underlie these triadic meta-liking perceptions, replicating previous results by Kenny et al. (1996). In a generalized round-robin study, unacquainted participants ( N = 403, 74.3% female, M age = 23.3) interacted and judged how much they liked others, were liked by others, and believed others liked each other. Analyses using the Triadic Social Relations Model revealed that judges somewhat agreed on who is liked and who likes whom, had some insight into who is generally liked and who likes whom, and relied on perceived reciprocity and assumed agreement, which were partially true. Beyond this, others were more accurate about how much one is liked, while one’s own and others’ perceptions about how much one is liked aligned to a certain degree.

articles.title: Increasing Support for Humanitarian Aid to Palestinian Civilians During the Israel–Gaza War Through Ideologically Tailored Social-Media Campaigns
articles.authors: Nimrod Nir, Eran Halperin
articles.abstract: Promoting support for humanitarian aid to an adversarial outgroup is difficult during active war. We introduce a digital field-experimental approach that embeds psychologically grounded interventions in people’s actual social-media environments. During the Israel–Gaza war, 6,105 adult Jewish Israeli Facebook users were assigned to a no-study-campaign control condition, a humanitarian-moral campaign emphasizing humanitarian obligation, or an instrumental-security campaign presenting aid as advancing Israeli security. Days after the campaigns ended, 4,784 participants completed the follow-up survey. Support for humanitarian aid declined in the control condition but increased under both campaigns, suggesting that psychological social-media interventions can buffer or reverse erosion of humanitarian attitudes during acute conflict. Political ideology moderated relative effectiveness: the instrumental-security campaign was especially effective among conservatives, whereas liberals responded positively to both. These findings provide partial support for ideological message matching and offer a scalable, ecologically valid framework for testing intergroup interventions in real-world settings.

articles.title: The Gambler’s Fallacy Fallacy Fallacy (Commentary on Xiang et al., 2025)
articles.authors: Daniel Banki, Uri Simonsohn
articles.abstract: Xiang et al. concluded that the gambler’s fallacy does not originate in biased beliefs. Reanalyzing their data, we arrived at the opposite conclusion. We show, more generally, that their main analysis—examining whether the median belief is biased—is not diagnostic of the presence of the gambler’s fallacy, whereas our test of the share of probability estimates for the streak ending above or below 50% is diagnostic. We also report results from a new study in which at least 80% of gambler’s-fallacy predictions originated in biased beliefs.

articles.title: High School Music Participation: The Role of Identity, Value, Expectancy, and Cost
articles.authors: Seth Pendergast, Peter Miksza
articles.abstract: While secondary music programs enjoy participation from many students, school music enrollment often does not reflect the demographics of the broader student population. This study examined how high-school students’ musical identities and sociocognitive beliefs influenced their intentions to enroll in high-school music classes. Drawing on situated expectancy-value theory, we developed a model of how musical identity and expectancy-value constructs influence students’ enrollment decisions in three music classes: large ensembles, music technology/production, and piano/guitar. We surveyed 486 students at a large U.S. public high school, measuring musical identity, expectancy-value constructs, and intentions to enroll in each of the three class contexts. Structural equation models showed musical identity positively predicted expectancy and value; expectancy negatively predicted cost; and both value and cost predicted enrollment intentions (positively and negatively, respectively). Notably, expectancy influenced intentions only indirectly via cost. Although both value and cost predicted intentions across all class types, cost was more strongly associated with intentions for large ensembles, whereas value was more strongly associated with intentions for music technology/production and piano/guitar. These findings suggest motivational beliefs are context-dependent and deeply interrelated. Music teachers may benefit from considering the context-specific roles of cost, value, and expectancy when recruiting students for classes.

articles.title: Mental Health Implications of (Mal-)Adaptive Approaches to Leisure Music Engagement: The Role of Motivation and Self-Criticism
articles.authors: Friederike Koehler, Julia Vigl, Suvi Saarikallio
articles.abstract: The relationship between music engagement and health has attracted growing academic interest over the past decades, pointing to mostly beneficial associations, especially with music listening and music interventions. However, recent research indicates a more complex relationship emphasizing the relevance of exploring how and why people engage with music. Since playing music and singing are common leisure-time activities for many people, this study aimed to investigate potential (mal-)adaptive approaches to music engagement, that is, self-determined motivation, and its association with mental health in amateur musicians. One hundred and ninety-eight participants completed an online survey on their motivation to make music, as well as depression, anxiety, stress, and self-criticism. Structural equation models showed that controlled motivation (more external reasons) positively predicted depression, stress, and self-criticism, but not anxiety. Further, results provided evidence for a full mediation of the association between controlled motivation and depression, anxiety, and stress via self-criticism. Our findings highlight the importance of individual motivations and dispositions in music engagement, pointing to potentially harmful effects on mental health. Practical implications for effective health promotion include considering individual motivations and dispositions and enhancing autonomy and self-compassion in leisure interventions and recreational therapy. Future research should investigate further individual and situational determinants.
